html:
The Germanic-speaking peoples who settled in eastern Britain after Roman rule ended and became the English. The map shows them in 500, in what is now eastern England and southeastern Scotland.

After the end of Roman rule in Britain around 410, settlers came across the North Sea from what is now northern Germany and Denmark. The monk Bede, writing around 731, names them as Angles, Saxons and Jutes. Ancient DNA shows a large movement of people who mixed with the Britons already there. In the west, British kingdoms held out.

The settlers formed kingdoms such as Kent, Wessex, Mercia, East Anglia and Northumbria. The ship burial at Sutton Hoo, from the early 7th century, shows the wealth of an East Anglian king. The Gregorian mission of 597 began their conversion to Christianity. Their language, Old English, is the language of Beowulf. Fighting the Vikings, Wessex united the English into one kingdom in 927, the start of England. The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended their rule.
